reason: CPU/GPU mini-batch pipeline scheduling explicitly designed for a single CPU+GPU host, so the adaptive-split policy is a clean tunable target; repo linked but artifact completeness and graph-dataset disk cost unverified.
LSM secondary indexing is squarely storage-engine work that fits the machine, but no repo was located, which violates the hard requirement.
ML-based DBMS knob/index tuning is only systems-adjacent, and the scout explicitly failed to find any artifact.
DBMS kernel composition is a database-architecture contribution rather than resource management, and gluing Arrow+Velox+ArrayFire from source without root is a heavy build for modest extension room.

CPU-offloaded attention and KV-cache management for online serving is exactly the single-GPU-plus-big-host regime of this machine, evaluated on GPUs weaker than the A5000, with obvious policy knobs (offload split, scheduling) to improve.
Metadata write-amplification work is good OS material, but it is framed as a distributed file-system service and no code was found.
Pure user-space bit-exact replay tooling with Ampere already validated runs trivially here, but numerical-reproducibility debugging is not a resource-management problem an OS course centers on.

DAG-aware request scheduling for LLM applications is core serving-systems work with clear policy headroom, but published results assume multi-GPU deployments and the research prototype's current state is unknown.
Adaptive execution and operator fusion over DuckDB is systems-adjacent, but end-to-end results hinge on external LLM API latency and cost, which this machine cannot control.
Trace-driven GPU-cluster scheduling simulator with a pinned artifact branch: exactly the kind of policy study one machine supports, with predictability/fairness knobs to extend.
Reproduction-friendly single-node benchmark suite, but learned query-optimizer cost models are DB-ML rather than an OS resource-management topic.

bpftime deliberately runs eBPF extensions in user space so the disabled-BPF machine is not a blocker, and the badged mature repo makes it buildable; MPK on Zen3 and root-requiring kernel baselines are the only risks.
Single-GPU join processing fits the hardware, but it is a query-processing algorithm with no located repo.
Self-contained CPU-only library with clear measurable baselines, but the work is decision-diagram data-structure engineering for verification, not systems resource management.

User-space SIMD content-defined chunking in the authors' own DedupBench builds with plain gcc and gives an obvious throughput/dedup-ratio hypothesis space; only the AVX-512 numbers are unreachable on Zen 3.
FL topology abstraction is a distributed-ML programming model rather than OS resource management, and the full system expects Docker/minikube so only the SDK path is usable.
Single-threaded user-space CPU chunking measured in MB/s on local files is a near-ideal machine fit, with the authors' DedupBench and a public dataset; only disk budget forces subsetting.
CPU thread orchestration is good OS material and 16 cores suffice, but no official repo was found and the MLP-aware decisions likely need blocked hardware counters.
Learned parameterized query optimization is DB-ML and no repo was located.
Tuning concurrent I/O to a single NVMe SSD from user space is core storage/I/O systems work that the two PM9A3 drives support directly, with concurrency-level heuristics to improve.
Memory-efficient approximate SSD indexing with an AE-badged artifact is strong OS content, but FTL-style evaluation usually rides on FEMU/KVM, so a pure trace-replay path must be confirmed.
Prefix-aware batching is exactly the LLM request-scheduling problem we want, but no repo was located and one path assumes two GPUs.
An online ski-rental policy deciding when a filter pays adaptation I/O is a small, released, user-space artifact with an obvious policy-swap hypothesis space.
Accuracy-aware maintenance scheduling is a reasonable policy target, but the paper's 800-core scale means everything must be re-done in simulation and the repo's simulation path is unverified.
CPU-only low-memory LLM serving is a fine single-node inference topic, but no repo was located.

Replacing the PyTorch caching allocator with lifetime-based planning is textbook memory management and the allocator itself can be exercised with small models, but the paper targets large-scale training so the headline savings need a scale-down.
Head-level KV-cache budget allocation is pure inference-time memory management on one GPU; the budget/attribution heuristic is an easy improvement axis, though artifact maturity is unknown.

Zenodo artifact and a training-free technique that runs on one GPU, but early-exit ranking for retrieval is an ML-inference optimization rather than OS resource management, and the paper targets edge hardware we lack.

Fine-grained expert offloading between 24 GB GPU and 125 GB host DRAM is precisely this machine's regime, with prefetch/caching policies to tune; small MoE models must be chosen and repo completeness is unverified.
A sketch-based approximate cache layer is a standalone user-space CPU module with obvious accuracy/memory trade-off knobs to extend.
A pure prefill-scheduling change with released code is an ideal hypothesis target, but only small or quantized MoEs fit 24 GB so the memory-traffic claim must be re-validated at reduced scale.
Anchor paper: trace-driven eviction study plus a C implementation in libCacheSim, CPU-only, with an open-ended policy-improvement space; only trace subsetting for disk is needed.
Widely used, easy-to-run user-space fuzzer, but compiler bug-finding is testing work rather than a systems-resource-management problem.
Very mature single-GPU artifact that scales down to 7B/13B on the A5000, but the contribution is weight quantization plus a kernel engine, closer to model compression than OS resource management.
At heart an importance-aware cache admission/eviction policy plus client scheduler with released code, giving good policy headroom; the thousands-of-simulated-clients scale needs a RAM/disk check.
Data-format reader generation inside the large Apache SystemDS tree is a narrow ingestion contribution with little OS-flavored extension room.

The trace-driven greedy allocation scheduler with released carbon traces and scaling profiles reproduces fully on one host; only the Kubernetes prototype path is closed without Docker or a second node.

GC write-amplification modeling for log-structured systems with a separately released user-space simulator and Zenodo archive is a complete, machine-friendly improvement target; only the FPGA prototype is out of reach.
RL-driven graph superoptimization is compiler-ML work and it depends on building the aging TASO CUDA/cuDNN stack, which is a real build risk on CUDA 11.8/driver 535.
In-memory KV concurrency control on multicore CPUs with a Zenodo AE artifact fits the 16-core host perfectly; extension space is real but narrower than a policy-rich system.

Single-GPU compiler extension generating FlashAttention-style kernels works on Ampere and has a clear baseline (FlexAttention), but kernel-codegen is systems-adjacent and Triton/Inductor version sensitivity is a build risk.
Fully trace-driven with a released dataset and prediction pipeline, but it is a field failure study whose only improvement axis is a better predictor, not a system change.

A software-only latency profiler that deliberately avoids hardware counters and kernel support matches this locked-down machine unusually well, but it requires a long custom LLVM-14 build and workload substitution for the kernel-bypass targets.
Floating-point execution verification is neither resource management nor released as code.
Computational-storage emulation is excellent OS material, but QEMU full-system emulation without /dev/kvm falls back to TCG and will likely be too slow for meaningful evaluation.
Compression plus direct query over compressed data is CPU-only and would fit trivially, but no repo was located.
Single-GPU user-space bit-flip injection already validated on consumer GPUs, but reliability for inference is a narrower topic and the reliable-memory abstraction may need emulation on the A5000.
CPU-trainable learned query optimizer with a linked repo, but plan-hint generation for PostgreSQL is DB-ML rather than OS resource management.
RocksDB-based single-node learned-index/LSM integration with an RL controller for SSTable sizing offers clear knob-swap hypotheses; artifact maturity of a small research repo is unverified.
A compact user-space C/C++ filter for KV stores that fits the machine trivially and has well-defined adaptation-policy variants to test.
Trace-driven DL-cluster scheduling on public Philly/Helios/Alibaba traces needs no cluster and has obvious policy swaps; repo quality and MILP solver licensing are unverified.
Single-machine in-memory graph index runs easily here, but filtered ANN search is an indexing algorithm rather than an OS resource-management problem.
Sketch-based timestamp storage in SplinterDB is genuine user-space storage systems work, but no repo was located.
Artifact and benchmark are released and the models fit 24 GB, but it is a prediction study for database profiling, so any improvement risks degenerating into pure reproduction.

User-space kernel-granularity GPU scheduling on a single GPU with a driver/CUDA version matching ours exactly, but it needs LLVM-14, Boost and a custom TVM fork all built from source, which is a long unprivileged build.
The analysis runs in user space so no kernel boot is needed, but fuzzing/bug-finding is not a resource-management topic and a per-user LLVM build plus long compiles eats the 10-week budget.

SSD-aware in-place vector-index rebalancing is great OS content, but the default SPDK path needs secure-boot/lockdown changes we cannot make, the RocksDB fallback is unverified, and the build relies on gcc-9 plus apt-only libs.
Maximizing NVMe bandwidth for SSD-resident embeddings matches the two PM9A3 drives, but an SPDK-style raw-device binding requirement would need root and force an io_uring reimplementation.
An adaptive bandit runtime layered over existing regex libraries builds without root and offers policy swaps, but regex query execution is far from OS resource management.
A cache admission/bypass mechanism in a CPU-only single-machine Python artifact is a clean policy-improvement target; the Docker-packaged dependencies must be replicated by hand with conda.
Trains and runs on one GPU with open code, but a learned cost model for tensor-program tuning is compiler-ML rather than an OS topic, and it rides on an aging TVM/Ansor stack.
Model-aware delta compression and tensor-level dedup is CPU-and-disk-only storage work with freely downloadable inputs, an excellent fit; only the petabyte-scale characterization must be scoped down.

Virtual-memory stitching inside the PyTorch caching allocator is classic memory management with an actively maintained repo; the A100-80GB workloads must be replaced by smaller models where fragmentation pressure may differ.

An importance-aware cache over the PyTorch DataLoader is a good policy target, but the multi-node multi-GPU setting and the assumed slow backing store both have to be emulated locally, changing the I/O-vs-compute balance the result depends on.
Thread-block-level GPU scheduling by intercepting CUDA in user space on a single GPU is an excellent machine fit and a natural home for new isolation/priority policies.
Single-GPU video-analytics configuration adaptation is an application-level ML pipeline, and the repo has no README and SLURM-oriented scripts, so setup cost is high.

Profiling application-defined resources on MariaDB/Redis is plausible here, but the tool samples hardware counters via perf, which perf_event_paranoid=3 blocks, leaving only part of the system reproducible.

Mature repo with a pinned AE branch and Zenodo archive, and single-GPU megakernels are the base case; but SM-level scheduling was tuned for newer architectures so Ampere without TMA/FP8 may need substantial retuning.
Learned group-level eviction evaluated by trace-driven simulation over 118 public traces, entirely CPU and user space, with named improvement axes (group formation, features, learning cadence).
Programmable operator scheduling is by construction a single-GPU contribution with released code integrated into six systems, giving a strong feasibility story and clear scheduling-policy headroom.
CPU/SIMD-only main-memory scan index runs anywhere, but it is an analytics index design with moderate extension room and unverified artifact completeness.
Badged Available+Functional+Reproduced Python instrumentation layer that mostly runs on one GPU, but invariant-based silent-error detection is reliability/testing rather than resource management.
The core mechanism depends on an AVX-512 instruction that this Zen 3 Threadripper lacks, so the headline result is unreproducible without writing an AVX2 fallback first.
CPU-only C++ library that builds easily, but an all-matches regex engine is an algorithms contribution with little OS-relevant extension space.
The FederatedScope-based artifact installs through conda and clients can be simulated on one host, but gradient-prediction for on-device FL is an ML-training technique, not OS resource management.

Pure user-space data-structure and memory-layout work benchmarked on real BGP dumps is an easy single-machine study, but IPv6 longest-prefix match is a networking data structure and the cache-level analysis needs blocked perf counters.

Single-node CPU-bound engine with datasets that fit the disk and an AE mirror, but the build is container-driven and must be ported, and the contribution is query-engine semantics rather than resource management.
Learned cost-model transferability is DB-ML and no artifact was found.
Policy generation is pure CPU work and the ImageNet model zoo fits 24 GB, giving a real scheduling-policy improvement space; the multi-GPU worker pool must be simulated or scaled to one GPU.
A small LM replacing a LIKE index path is a database-ML idea with no located repo.
